def: The extra energy a ring carries compared with a strain-free chain of the same atoms. It is the sum of angle strain, torsional strain and steric strain. Cyclopropane and cyclobutane have the most; cyclohexane in a chair has none.

The energy change when a compound is made from its elements, in kcal/mol. Dividing a ring's value by its number of CH₂ groups lets rings be compared: cyclohexane is −4.9 per CH₂, the same as a strain-free chain, while cyclopropane is +4.2 and cyclobutane +1.7. The gap from −4.9 is the strain per CH₂.
The cost of forcing bond angles away from the 109.5° an sp3 carbon prefers. Cyclopropane's 60° angles are the extreme case.
The cost of eclipsed bonds on neighbouring atoms: the electrons in the bonds repel when they line up. Staggered bonds have none.
The cost of pushing atoms or groups closer together than their size allows. A 1,3-diaxial interaction is steric strain.

To do with the space that atoms and groups take up. Steric strain is the energy cost when groups are pushed too close together, as for an axial methyl. Steric hindrance is bulk that blocks a reagent's approach: the lecture's 'low sterics' for SN2 means little hindrance at the carbon being attacked, as in methyl and primary.
Bulk around a reacting atom that physically blocks the approach of a reagent. It is why SN2 slows from methyl to primary to secondary and stops at tertiary.
A shape a molecule takes by rotating about single bonds. Conformations interconvert without breaking any bond, so they are the same compound.
A drawing that looks straight down one carbon-carbon bond: the front carbon is a dot, the back carbon a circle, and the three bonds on each show the angles between them.
The angle between a bond on the front atom and a bond on the back atom when you look down the bond that joins them: 60° is gauche, 180° is anti, 0° is eclipsed.
A conformation in which the bonds on the back atom sit between the bonds on the front atom (dihedral angles of 60°). It has no torsional strain.
A conformation in which the bonds on the front and back atoms line up (dihedral angle 0°), so each hides the one behind it. It has the most torsional strain.

Staggered, with two groups 60° apart. One gauche pair of methyl groups costs about 0.9 kcal/mol of steric strain. An axial methyl on cyclohexane is gauche to two ring carbons, which is why it costs twice that: 1.74 kcal/mol.

Staggered, with two groups 180° apart, on opposite sides. It is the lowest-energy arrangement of two large groups, as in anti butane. In E2 the hydrogen and the leaving group must be anti to each other (anti-periplanar).
The three-carbon ring. Its 60° angles and fully eclipsed hydrogens make it the most strained simple ring; its carbon-carbon bonds bend outward (banana bonds).

A carbon-carbon bond of cyclopropane. The sp3 orbitals cannot point along the 60° lines between the carbons, so they overlap off-axis, outside the triangle. Less overlap means a weaker bond: 65 kcal/mol, against 88 in propane.
The four-carbon ring. It puckers slightly, like a butterfly (the lecture gives an angle of 88°), trading a little more angle strain for less eclipsing.

Bent out of flat. Cyclobutane puckers (the lecture gives an angle of 88°, not 90°) because a flat ring would have eight eclipsed C-H pairs: bending relieves some torsional strain at the cost of a little more angle strain.
The five-carbon ring. Its angles are close to ideal, so its strain is mostly torsional; it bends into an envelope or a half-chair to stagger some of its bonds.
The shape of cyclopentane: four carbons in a plane and the fifth bent out of it, like the flap of an envelope.
The six-carbon ring. In its chair conformation every angle is close to 109.5° and every bond is staggered, so it has no ring strain.
The lowest-energy shape of cyclohexane: no angle strain and no torsional strain. Each carbon has one axial and one equatorial position.

A higher-energy shape of cyclohexane with eclipsed bonds along its sides and two flagpole hydrogens that crowd each other. The twist-boat is its slightly more stable, twisted form. The ring passes through them during a ring flip.

In the lecture, one of the two low-energy shapes of cyclopentane (the other is the envelope): three carbons in a plane, with one above it and one below. The same name is also used for the highest-energy point of cyclohexane's ring flip, where part of the ring is flattened.

A bond on a chair that points straight up or straight down, parallel to the ring's axis. Axial positions alternate up, down, up, down around the ring, and an axial group is crowded by the two axial hydrogens on its own face.
parts: axle: the line a wheel turns on

def: A bond on a chair that points outward around the ring's middle, roughly in the plane of the ring. Equatorial groups have more room, so large groups prefer this position.

The change of one chair into the other. Every axial group becomes equatorial and every equatorial group becomes axial, but up stays up and down stays down. It happens many thousands of times a second at room temperature.
The crowding between an axial group and the two axial hydrogens on the same face, two carbons away on each side (positions 3 and 5). It is what makes the axial position cost energy.

The energy cost of putting a group axial instead of equatorial on cyclohexane, in kcal/mol. From the lecture's table: methyl 1.74, ethyl 1.79, isopropyl 2.61, tert-butyl 5.5. The larger the A-value, the more the group insists on being equatorial.
On the same side. On a ring: two groups on the same face, both up or both down, which says nothing by itself about axial or equatorial. On a double bond: two groups on the same side of the C=C.

On opposite sides. On a ring: two groups on opposite faces, one up and one down, which says nothing by itself about axial or equatorial. On a double bond: two groups on opposite sides of the C=C; a trans alkene is usually more stable than its cis isomer.
The group C(CH₃)₃. It is so large that a ring carrying it stays almost entirely in the chair that puts it equatorial, so it is said to lock the ring.
A solid wedge bond points toward you (up, on a ring drawn flat); a dashed bond points away from you (down).
An atom or group attached to a ring or chain in place of a hydrogen.
Both groups axial. A trans-1,2, cis-1,3 or trans-1,4 pair is diaxial in one chair and diequatorial (both equatorial) in the other, and the diequatorial chair is the stable one.

Nuclear magnetic resonance. Nuclei such as ¹H behave like tiny magnets; in a strong magnetic field they absorb radio waves at a frequency that depends on their surroundings, so each kind of hydrogen in a molecule reports itself.
Where a signal appears in an NMR spectrum, in parts per million (ppm, the δ scale) from the reference TMS at 0. Hydrogens near electronegative atoms or pi bonds appear at higher ppm.

Hydrogens in the same environment, which give one NMR signal together. Test: replace each in turn with another atom; if you get the same compound (or its mirror image), they are equivalent. Symmetry is what makes hydrogens equivalent.
One peak, or group of peaks, in an NMR spectrum. Each set of equivalent hydrogens gives one signal, so counting signals means counting the different kinds of hydrogen.

Electrons around a nucleus oppose the magnet's field and shield the nucleus, so its signal appears upfield (lower ppm). A nearby electronegative atom pulls electron density away and deshields it, moving the signal downfield (higher ppm).
Toward higher ppm, the left side of an NMR spectrum, where deshielded hydrogens appear. Upfield is toward lower ppm, the right side.
Tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄, the reference compound for NMR. Its twelve equivalent, strongly shielded hydrogens define 0 ppm.
The area under an NMR signal. It is proportional to the number of hydrogens that give the signal, so the areas give the ratio of the kinds of hydrogen.
An imaginary mirror that cuts a molecule into two halves that are reflections of each other. Atoms that the mirror swaps are equivalent, which is why symmetric molecules give fewer NMR signals.

The division of one NMR signal into several lines by the hydrogens on the neighbouring carbons. The n + 1 rule: a hydrogen with n equivalent neighbours on the next carbon appears as n + 1 lines. One neighbour gives a doublet; six give a septet.
An NMR signal split into seven lines. By the n + 1 rule it belongs to a hydrogen with six equivalent neighbours: the CH of an isopropyl group, which sits next to two CH₃ groups.
A species that gives up a proton (H⁺). A Brønsted base is a species that accepts one.

A species that gives up a proton (Brønsted) or accepts an electron pair (Lewis). Its strength is measured by its pKa: the lower the pKa, the stronger the acid. To compare two acids, compare how stable their conjugate bases are.

A species that accepts a proton (Brønsted) or donates an electron pair (Lewis). Its strength is read from the pKa of its conjugate acid: the higher that pKa, the stronger the base. In the lecture: HS⁻ < HO⁻ < H₂N⁻ < H₃C⁻.
A species that accepts an electron pair. Every electrophile is a Lewis acid: in the lecture, the δ⁺ hydrogen of H-Cl and the δ⁺ carbon of CH₃Cl.
A species that donates an electron pair. Every nucleophile is a Lewis base: in the lecture, HO⁻ attacking the δ⁺ carbon of CH₃Cl.
What is left of an acid after it loses its proton. The more stable the conjugate base, the stronger the acid.
What a base becomes when it accepts a proton: the conjugate acid of HO⁻ is H₂O. The stronger the base, the weaker its conjugate acid, which means the higher that acid's pKa.
A number that measures how strong an acid is: pKa = −log Ka. The lower the pKa, the stronger the acid, and each unit is a factor of ten. A strong acid has a weak conjugate base.
The acid dissociation constant: the equilibrium constant for an acid giving its proton to water. A large Ka means a strong acid.

The ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium. For a proton transfer, Keq is 10 to the power of (pKa of the acid formed minus pKa of the acid you started with), so the equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid, the one with the higher pKa.
How strongly an atom pulls bonding electrons toward itself. Across a row, a more electronegative atom holds a negative charge better: that is why HF is a stronger acid than H₂O, NH₃ or CH₄.

The pull (or push) of electron density through sigma bonds by a nearby electronegative atom or group. It stabilizes a negative charge and fades quickly with distance: trifluoroacetic acid is far stronger than acetic acid.

Describing one species by two or more Lewis structures that differ only in where the electrons are. Spreading a charge over several atoms (delocalization) stabilizes it: a carboxylate shares its charge between two oxygens.

R-CO₂H. Its pKa is about 4 in the lecture, far below an alcohol's 16, because its conjugate base, the carboxylate, shares the negative charge between two oxygens by resonance. Three fluorines add induction: CF₃CO₂H is −1.5.

R-CO₂⁻, the conjugate base of a carboxylic acid. Its charge is shared equally by two oxygens (resonance), which makes it a stable, weak base and only a modest nucleophile: acetate is 630 in the lecture's table, against 16,000 for hydroxide.
How easily an atom's electron cloud is distorted. Large atoms such as iodine and sulfur are polarizable: they spread out a charge, which makes their acids stronger, and they are good nucleophiles.

R-SH, the sulfur version of an alcohol (a sulfide, R-S-R, is the sulfur version of an ether). Sulfur is larger than oxygen and spreads out a negative charge, so H₂S (10 in the lecture) is a stronger acid than water (15.7). The conjugate base, HS⁻ or a thiolate RS⁻, is a weak base but an excellent nucleophile: 126,000 in the lecture's table.

A compound with nitrogen bonded to carbon, R-NH₂. Its lone pair makes it a base and a nucleophile (NH₃ is 8,000 in the lecture's table). Its N-H is a very weak acid, pKa 38, so its conjugate base, the amide ion NH₂⁻, is a very strong base. Adding a proton to an amine gives an ammonium ion, R-NH₃⁺.

The mixing of s and p orbitals on an atom: sp3 (four groups, 109.5°), sp2 (three groups, 120°), sp (two groups, 180°). More s character holds electrons closer to the nucleus, so an sp C-H (an alkyne, pKa about 25) is far more acidic than an sp3 C-H (about 55 in the lecture's table).

The anion HC≡C⁻ or RC≡C⁻, the conjugate base of a terminal alkyne (pKa 25). Its lone pair is in an sp orbital with 50% s character, held close to the nucleus, so it is far more stable than an sp3 carbanion. It is still a strong base, and an excellent nucleophile: 126,000 in the lecture's table.

The group that departs with the pair of electrons from its bond to carbon. Good leaving groups are weak bases, the conjugate bases of strong acids: iodide, bromide, chloride, tosylate, water. Hydroxide and alkoxides are poor ones.
The group OTs (p-toluenesulfonate). Turning an alcohol's OH into OTs makes an excellent leaving group, because the charge on the departing tosylate is shared by three oxygens.
The arrow used in mechanisms. It shows a pair of electrons moving: its tail starts at a lone pair or a bond, and its head points to the atom or bond where the electrons end up.
A pair of valence electrons on one atom that is not shared in a bond. Lone pairs are where most curved arrows start.
The charge assigned to an atom in a Lewis structure: its valence electrons, minus its lone-pair electrons, minus one for each bond.
An acid-base step: a base uses an electron pair to take H⁺ from an acid. It is usually the fastest step in a mechanism.
A compound with a carbon-metal bond, such as RLi or RMgX. Carbon is more electronegative than the metal, so the carbon is electron rich: a strong nucleophile and a very strong base.

An organomagnesium halide, RMgX, made from an alkyl halide and magnesium metal in an ether solvent. It behaves like a carbanion R⁻: it attacks electrophilic carbon and is destroyed by any acidic hydrogen, even that of water or an alcohol.
A compound RLi, made from an alkyl halide and two equivalents of lithium metal. Like a Grignard reagent it acts as a carbanion: a strong nucleophile and a very strong base.
A carbon with a lone pair and a negative charge. Alkyl carbanions are among the strongest bases there are, because their conjugate acids, the alkanes, have a pKa of about 55 in the lecture's table.

A compound with an oxygen between two carbons, R-O-R. Diethyl ether is the lecture's solvent for making a Grignard reagent (THF is also used): it has no acidic hydrogen, and its oxygen lone pairs stabilize the magnesium. The lecture makes organolithium reagents in pentane instead.
The isotope of hydrogen with one neutron, written D. Adding D₂O to an organometallic puts a D exactly where the carbon-metal bond was, which shows which carbon carried the negative charge.

A compound with a halogen (F, Cl, Br or I) on an sp3 carbon. It is the usual substrate for substitution and elimination, and is classed as methyl, primary, secondary or tertiary by how many carbons are attached to the carbon that holds the halogen.

A primary carbon (1°) is attached to one other carbon. A primary alkyl halide is fast in SN2 (ethyl 0.033 against methyl 1) and does no SN1 or E1, because a primary carbocation is too unstable to form unless it is allylic or benzylic. Only a bulky strong base turns it to E2.

A secondary carbon (2°) is attached to two other carbons. A secondary alkyl halide can react by all four mechanisms, so the reagent and the solvent decide: SN2 is slow (isopropyl 8.3 × 10⁻⁴ against methyl 1), a strong base gives E2, and a weak base in a polar protic solvent gives SN1 and E1.

A tertiary carbon (3°) is attached to three other carbons. A tertiary alkyl halide does no SN2 (too much steric hindrance: relative rate 0). It forms the most stable carbocation, so it is the fastest in SN1 and E1, and it gives E2 with a strong base.
On the carbon next to a C=C double bond. An allylic cation is stabilized by resonance, and allylic halides are fast in both SN1 and SN2.
On the carbon attached directly to a benzene ring. A benzylic position is activated like an allylic one: its cation is stabilized by resonance with the ring.
On a carbon of a C=C double bond itself. Vinylic halides, and aryl halides (halogen on a benzene ring), do not react by SN1 or SN2.

An electron-rich species that uses an electron pair to form a bond to an electron-poor atom, usually carbon. Nucleophiles are Lewis bases: anions such as HO⁻, CN⁻ and I⁻, or neutral molecules with lone pairs such as NH₃ and H₂O.
An electron-poor species that accepts an electron pair from a nucleophile. The carbon that holds a leaving group is an electrophile, because the leaving group pulls electron density away from it.

How fast a species attacks carbon: a rate (kinetics), measured in the lecture by the relative rate of an SN2 reaction. It often runs with basicity, but not always: large, polarizable atoms such as I⁻ and HS⁻ are strong nucleophiles and weak bases, and a bulkier nucleophile is a poorer one. In the lecture's sketch it increases to the left and down the periodic table.

How strongly a species holds a proton: an equilibrium (thermodynamics), read from the pKa of its conjugate acid. In the lecture's sketch basicity increases to the left and up the periodic table: HS⁻ < HO⁻ < H₂N⁻ < H₃C⁻. Nucleophilicity is a rate instead, and increases to the left and down.
A reaction in which one group on a carbon is replaced by another: a nucleophile takes the place of a leaving group.

Substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular. One step: the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group as the leaving group leaves. Rate = k[substrate][nucleophile]. The configuration inverts. Methyl and primary are fastest; tertiary does not react.
The approach of the nucleophile in SN2: from directly behind the carbon, 180° from the leaving group. Anything bulky on that side slows the reaction.

The result of backside attack: the three other groups on the carbon flip to the other side, like an umbrella in the wind, so a stereocenter ends up with the opposite arrangement. Also called Walden inversion.
The product keeps the same three-dimensional arrangement at the stereocenter as the starting material. SN1 gives a mixture of retention and inversion.
Happening in a single step: all the bond making and bond breaking occur together, through one transition state and with no intermediate. SN2 and E2 are concerted.

The highest-energy point along one step of a reaction, where bonds are partly made and partly broken. It cannot be isolated. It is drawn in brackets with a double dagger (‡), partial bonds dashed and partial charges marked δ.
A real species formed in one step and used up in the next. It sits in a valley on the energy diagram, between two transition states. A carbocation is the intermediate of SN1 and E1.
The energy climb from the reactants to the transition state of a step. The higher it is, the slower the step.
The slowest step of a mechanism, the one with the highest transition state. Only the species involved up to and including it appear in the rate law. In SN1 and E1 it is the loss of the leaving group.
The equation that says how the rate depends on concentrations. SN2 and E2: rate = k[substrate][nucleophile or base]. SN1 and E1: rate = k[substrate] only.
Two species take part in the rate-determining step, so the rate depends on both concentrations. It is the 2 in SN2 and E2.
Only one species takes part in the rate-determining step, so the rate depends on the substrate alone. It is the 1 in SN1 and E1.

A plot of energy against the progress of a reaction. Peaks are transition states and valleys are intermediates; the height of a peak sets the rate, and the difference between the two ends sets the equilibrium. A one-step reaction has one peak; SN1 and E1 have two.

A transition state looks most like the species it is closest to in energy. For an uphill step, such as forming a carbocation, the transition state resembles the product, so whatever stabilizes the carbocation also lowers the barrier.
A polar solvent with an O-H or N-H bond, such as water, methanol or ethanol. It hydrogen-bonds to anions, which slows nucleophiles (small ones most) and stabilizes ions, so it favours SN1 and E1.

A polar solvent with no O-H or N-H bond, such as DMSO, DMF, acetone or acetonitrile. It solvates cations but leaves anions bare, so nucleophiles are much more reactive: these are the best solvents for SN2.
The surrounding of a dissolved ion or molecule by solvent molecules. A tightly solvated anion, caged by hydrogen bonds, must shed solvent before it can attack, so it is a weaker nucleophile.
The attraction between a hydrogen on O, N or F and a lone pair on another O, N or F. It is how protic solvents hold on to anions.

Making an ether by SN2: an alkoxide (RO⁻) attacks a methyl or primary alkyl halide. Of the two ways to split the target ether, choose the one in which the halide is the less hindered piece; a hindered halide gives elimination instead.

RO⁻, the conjugate base of an alcohol, made with sodium metal or sodium hydride. It is both a strong base and a good nucleophile, so it substitutes on unhindered halides and eliminates on hindered ones.
Within one molecule. When the nucleophile and the leaving group are in the same molecule, SN2 closes a ring; three-, five- and six-membered rings form fastest.
Between two separate molecules.
A three-membered ring containing one oxygen. It forms when an alkoxide attacks, from the back, the neighbouring carbon that holds a leaving group: an intramolecular SN2.
An atom, usually a carbon with four different groups, at which swapping two groups gives a different stereoisomer. Its arrangement is labelled R or S.
The fixed three-dimensional arrangement of groups at a stereocenter (R or S) or a double bond (E or Z). Unlike a conformation, it changes only if a bond is broken.
Compounds with the same atoms joined in the same order but arranged differently in space. Two stereoisomers are either enantiomers (mirror images) or diastereomers (not mirror images).

Not superimposable on its mirror image, like a left and a right hand. A chiral molecule has an enantiomer. A carbon with four different groups (a chiral centre, or stereocentre) usually makes a molecule chiral.

Superimposable on its mirror image, so it has no enantiomer. A molecule with a plane of symmetry is achiral. The lecture's example is cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane: its two chairs are mirror images, but a ring flip turns one into the other.

Stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other and cannot be superimposed. Every stereocenter is inverted from one to the other. They have identical physical properties except for the direction in which they rotate polarized light.

Stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other: some, but not all, of their stereocenters differ, or they are cis and trans isomers. They have different physical properties and different energies.
A 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers. It does not rotate polarized light. SN1 at a stereocenter gives a nearly racemic product, because the flat carbocation is attacked from either face.
lit: from grapes: racemic acid, the first such mixture studied, came from wine making

def: The stereochemistry of the starting material fixes the stereochemistry of the product: a different stereoisomer in gives a different stereoisomer out. SN2 (inversion) and E2 (anti-periplanar) are stereospecific.

Forms one stereoisomer in preference to another when both are possible. An elimination that could give either geometric isomer of an alkene usually gives more of the more stable one, with its large groups on opposite sides.
Forms the bond or double bond at one position in preference to another. Zaitsev's rule and the Hofmann product describe the regioselectivity of elimination.

Substitution, nucleophilic, unimolecular. Two steps: the leaving group leaves to give a carbocation (slow), then the nucleophile adds to either face (fast). Rate = k[substrate]. Tertiary is fastest; it goes with a weak nucleophile in a polar protic solvent, and it gives a mixture of inversion and retention.

A carbon with three bonds, six valence electrons and a positive charge. It is sp2 and flat, with an empty p orbital. Stability: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, and allylic or benzylic cations are stabilized by resonance. It is the intermediate of SN1 and E1.

The breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group, with both electrons going to the leaving group, to give a carbocation and an anion. It is the first step, and the slow step, of SN1 and E1. A more polar solvent speeds it up by stabilizing the ions as they form.

The sharing of electrons from a neighbouring C-H or C-C sigma bond into an empty p orbital. Each alkyl group on a carbocation adds this stabilization, which is why tertiary cations are the most stable.

A rearrangement in which a hydrogen moves, with its pair of bonding electrons, from the carbon next door to a carbocation. It happens when it turns the carbocation into a more stable one, for example secondary into tertiary.

A rearrangement in which an alkyl group, usually methyl, moves with its bonding electrons to the neighbouring carbocation carbon to give a more stable carbocation. It is the usual choice when the neighbouring carbon has no hydrogen to give, as next to a carbon with four carbon groups. When the group that moves is a ring carbon, the ring grows by one: a ring expansion.

A carbocation rearrangement in which a ring bond moves to a cationic carbon just outside the ring, so the ring gains one carbon. A cation next to a four-membered ring becomes a cyclopentyl cation, which also relieves ring strain: the lecture's homework with (1-bromoethyl)cyclobutane.
A change in the carbon skeleton or in the position of the charge during a mechanism. Any reaction that goes through a carbocation (SN1, E1) can rearrange; SN2 and E2 never do.
A substitution in which the solvent itself is the nucleophile, as when a tertiary halide reacts in water or an alcohol. It is the typical SN1 reaction.

Elimination, unimolecular. Two steps: the leaving group leaves to give a carbocation (slow), then a weak base removes a hydrogen from the carbon next door to form the double bond. Rate = k[substrate]. It competes with SN1, is favoured by heat, and gives mainly the Zaitsev alkene.
A reaction in which a hydrogen and a leaving group are lost from neighbouring carbons and a pi bond forms between them.

Elimination, bimolecular. One step: a strong base removes a beta hydrogen while the double bond forms and the leaving group leaves. Rate = k[substrate][base]. The hydrogen and the leaving group must be anti-periplanar.

Elimination, unimolecular, conjugate base: the base removes the hydrogen first to give a carbanion, and the leaving group leaves afterwards. The lecture calls E2 with a poor leaving group such as fluoride E1cb-like: the C-H bond breaks ahead of the C-F bond, the transition state has carbanion character, and the Hofmann alkene wins (70%).

The geometry E2 requires: the hydrogen being removed and the leaving group lie in one plane on opposite sides of the C-C bond, a dihedral angle of 180°. On a cyclohexane ring this means both must be axial.
lit: on opposite sides, about in one plane

def: The hydrogen and the leaving group in one plane on the same side of the C-C bond, a dihedral angle of 0°. The lecture's point: orbital overlap is not optimal and the conformation is eclipsed, so the transition state is less stable and E2 goes through the anti-periplanar arrangement instead.
lit: on the same side, about in one plane

def: The arrangement E2 needs on a cyclohexane ring: the leaving group axial, and a hydrogen on the neighbouring carbon axial on the opposite face. If the leaving group is axial only in the less stable chair, the reaction is slow.
A hydrogen on a carbon next to the carbon that holds the leaving group. The carbon with the leaving group is alpha; its neighbours are beta. Elimination removes a beta hydrogen.

The carbon that holds the leaving group. The carbons bonded to it are the beta carbons. In SN2 the nucleophile attacks the alpha carbon from the back, and more branching on the alpha and beta carbons favours E2 over SN2.

A carbon bonded to the alpha carbon, the carbon that holds the leaving group. Its hydrogens are beta hydrogens, and E2 removes one of them. A methyl halide has no beta carbon, so it cannot react by E2.
Elimination usually gives mainly the more substituted alkene, the one with more carbon groups on its double-bond carbons, because it is the more stable.

The less substituted alkene. In the lecture it becomes the major E2 product when the leaving group is poor: with fluoride, 2-hexyl-F gives 70% 1-hexene, so F is called a Hofmann leaving group (an E1cb-like E2). A bulky base such as potassium tert-butoxide also favours it, because it reaches the least hindered hydrogen more easily.

A strong base whose size makes it a poor nucleophile (the lecture's words for tert-butoxide), such as potassium tert-butoxide, (CH₃)₃CO⁻ K⁺. It can still do SN2 on a methyl halide such as CH₃I, which is wide open, but with primary, secondary and tertiary halides it gives E2, and it favours the Hofmann product.

A hydrocarbon with a carbon-carbon double bond. The more carbon groups on the double-bond carbons, the more stable the alkene (tetrasubstituted > trisubstituted > disubstituted > monosubstituted), and trans is more stable than cis.

Alkenes with the same atoms joined in the same order that differ in which side of the double bond their groups are on. A double bond does not rotate, so they are different compounds (diastereomers). They are named cis and trans, or E (higher-priority groups on opposite sides) and Z (same side).
The second bond of a double bond, formed by sideways overlap of two p orbitals. Its electrons lie above and below the plane of the atoms.

A bond formed by head-on overlap of two orbitals, with its electrons on the line between the two atoms. Every single bond is a sigma bond, and a double bond is one sigma bond plus one pi bond. Groups can rotate about a sigma bond, which is what makes conformations possible.
Elimination of H-X from an alkyl halide to give an alkene.
The molecule the reagent acts on. In substitution and elimination it is the compound that carries the leaving group.

A base whose conjugate acid is a weak acid (high pKa): hydroxide, alkoxides, amide (NH₂⁻), carbanions. On the flowchart a strong base gives E2 with secondary and tertiary substrates; with a primary one only a bulky strong base does.

A base whose conjugate acid is a fairly strong acid (low pKa). The flowchart has two kinds: weak bases that are good nucleophiles, such as I⁻ and HS⁻, which give SN2; and weak bases that are poor nucleophiles, such as water and alcohols, which leave SN1 and E1.
